analysis.one_liner: Restores 2009-level estate and gift taxes on large inheritances and puts the revenue into Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate and attracted zero cosponsors before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the estate tax back to the rates and exemptions in effect in 2009: a top rate of 45 percent on estates above $3.5 million (about $7 million for a married couple), and tighter gift tax rules. It would merge Social Security's two trust funds into one and deposit all estate and gift tax revenue into that fund, using money from inherited fortunes to shore up retirement and disability benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries, roughly the tens of millions of retirees, disabled workers, and survivors who draw benefits. The new estate tax revenue would extend how long the trust fund can pay full scheduled benefits before across-the-board cuts would otherwise be needed. It also falls only on the largest estates, since a $3.5 million exemption per spouse shields almost all families entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees, survivors, and disabled workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the top estate and gift tax rate to 45 percent and lowers the tax-free exemption to $3.5 million per person, returning both to the levels in effect in 2009, with the changes applying to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2019.

It combines the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund and directs that 100 percent of estate and gift tax revenue be appropriated into that fund, adding a new revenue stream funded by the largest inherited fortunes.

analysis.who_pays: The wealthiest households. Only estates exceeding $3.5 million per spouse would owe more, and the reduction in the lifetime gift exemption to $1 million would make it harder to move large fortunes to heirs tax-free while alive. Nearly all families — roughly the bottom 99 percent or more of estates — would pay no additional estate tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Inheritances above about $7 million per couple

drawbacks.text: Small business owners and farm families whose wealth is tied up in land or equipment rather than cash could face a tax bill at death, which is the standard objection to a lower estate exemption; in practice, the $3.5 million per-person exemption means this applies only to farms and businesses worth several million dollars.

The bill raises no new general revenue and its solvency benefit is limited: even 2009-level estate taxes generate tens of billions a year against Social Security's multi-trillion-dollar funding gap, so it would extend the trust fund but not fully close the shortfall.
Critics of the estate tax argue it taxes wealth that was already taxed when earned, and that it can force fire sales of illiquid assets like businesses or land to pay the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on a very small group — heirs of estates over $3.5 million per spouse — while the benefit flows to every Social Security beneficiary through a more solvent trust fund. The main honest caveat is that the revenue is not large enough on its own to permanently fix Social Security's finances, so it is a partial fix, not a complete one. The 2009 exemption levels were high enough that family farms and small businesses below roughly $7 million per couple are untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee in June 2019, and the committee never held a vote on it or sent it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on June 25, 2019.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, which was the only action it ever received.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress.
The Finance Committee took no further action, so the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 without a committee vote, a floor vote, or a House companion moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs to the largest estates came out ahead: they kept the higher, 2019-law exemption and 40 percent top rate instead of the 45 percent rate and $3.5 million exemption this bill would have imposed, and Social Security received no new dedicated revenue from inherited wealth.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; recruited no cosponsors over 18 months.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over estate and gift taxes
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote after it was referred, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and no Republican or Democratic cosponsor joined, and the Republican-controlled Senate agenda never reached it.

industries.note: The bill would raise their estate and gift tax bills to 2009 levels, costing large inheritances roughly 45 cents per dollar above $3.5 million per spouse. Keeping the 2019 rules preserves roughly $11 million per couple in tax-free transfers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Higher estate tax rates and lower exemptions increase demand for trust, gift, and valuation planning among wealthy clients. Its business grows when the tax it helps clients avoid is larger.
